_about: Judgements read by tools/clue_shapes.py; the tool never writes this file. `patterns` are tried in order, first match wins, after an exact `shapes` entry. A pattern is a regular expression over the skeleton (tools/clue_shapes.py docstring) with optional depth_min/depth_max (nesting of the skeleton's brackets) and mech_min/mech_max (non-charade ops). verdict is one of ok, rare, redundant, mislabelled, implausible, unverified. `why` says what is wrong, `right` the shape it should have; `note` (exact shapes) is printed under the top-80 table. A skeleton of at least 150 clues matching nothing is listed at the top of docs/CLUE_SHAPES.md.

DD.note: a double definition: two definitions, no wordplay, the one family with no tree

cdef(V,V).why: a cryptic definition with the clue split into its two halves
cdef(V,V).note: the clue split into the literal half and the cryptic half; the grammar's cd([words]) is one block, so two disjoint halves are tolerated, not required

del(S,B).note: the removed letters are stored bare (no clue words), as a head, tail or inner deletion of a few letters; legitimate, but a positional deletion (first/last letter) carries its meaning only in the indicator

ins(ins(S,A),A).why: two things inserted into one outer word
ins(ins(S,A),A).note: one outer word with two inserts but, in nearly every clue, an indicator on the outer container only: the inner container is unindicated, so the tree says 'inside' twice for one phrase; a single container with a charade as its inner arm is the other way to write it

(S+S).note: the plain charade of two synonyms

ana(V).note: the plain anagram of clue words

patterns.name: cryptic definition whose parts repeat each other
patterns.why: a cryptic definition stored as two or three leaves where one is the whole clue (or the clue said twice) and the other a span of it, so the same words are claimed twice
patterns.right: cdef over the clue words once; the surface and cryptic readings belong in the leaf's note

patterns.name: anagram of a charade of verbatim words
patterns.why: the fodder is cut into word-by-word leaves joined by an unindicated charade, which says nothing a single multi-word fodder leaf does not; the charade is not a mechanism here, it is the fodder written in pieces
patterns.right: ana(V): one leaf holding all the fodder words

patterns.name: reversal and anagram stacked
patterns.why: an anagram's output order is free, so reversing it (or anagramming a reversal) adds nothing; in these clues the reverse indicator really sits on a different piece, or the intermediate word is an invented string
patterns.right: one anagram over the fodder, with the reversal on its own sibling piece if there is one

patterns.name: letter selection over another selection or op
patterns.why: a pick made from the result of another operation (first of the outer letters, first of the middle); a setter writes one selection, so this is a two-step the clue does not print, or a leaf that swallowed an indicator
patterns.right: one selection op over the fodder words, or the picks as separate pieces of a charade

patterns.name: same letter selection repeated word by word
patterns.why: an acrostic (heads of each word, tails, middles) built as one op per word inside a charade, usually with the indicator on the first op only, where the clue means one pick across a phrase
patterns.right: one first/last/mid/outer/nth op over a single multi-word leaf

patterns.name: charade directly inside a charade
patterns.why: a charade is associative, so a bracketed charade inside a charade changes nothing; most carry a trailing unchecked leaf of leftover words
patterns.right: one flat charade (or an indicator on the whole charade)

patterns.name: wordplay that is one synonym leaf
patterns.why: a tree of a single leaf is no wordplay at all: it restates the answer as one 'synonym' of the clue words, or is a cross-reference ('See 1')
patterns.right: a cryptic definition, a double definition, or a real parse; a cross-reference belongs to the linked group

patterns.name: anagram wrapped around a container
patterns.why: the anagram is stored outside the container, as the last step, but the clues work the other way: a synonym or word is the container and an anagram of clue words goes inside it (FLYPITCH: LYP, an anagram of 'ply', inside FITCH, 'fur'; SECRETARIATE: CRETA, an anagram of 'crate', inside SERIATE). Almost all are unchecked, so nothing refused the wrong nesting
patterns.right: ins(outer, ana(V)): the anagram is the container's inner arm

patterns.name: answer letters with no clue words in a charade
patterns.why: a charade piece (or fodder piece) made of letters no clue word supplies: an unexplained gap in the parse, not a mechanism
patterns.right: the leaf for the clue word that supplies them (an abbreviation or a selection)

patterns.name: palindrome with its definition or indicator stored as leaves
patterns.why: the palindrome op wraps unchecked leaves that are the definition and the indicator rather than letters
patterns.right: pal<indicator>([fodder]) or pal() over the answer alone

patterns.name: indirect anagram (fodder is a synonym)
patterns.why: the anagram's fodder is another word's synonym, which only Azed, Mephisto and a few toughies expect solvers to find; in daily puzzles it is an error unless the clue flags it, and in many of these the leaf has simply respelled the printed words
patterns.right: ana(V) over the printed words when the leaf only dropped a link word or respelled; a deliberate indirect anagram stays

patterns.name: letter selection from a synonym
patterns.why: an initial, ending or middle taken from a synonym rather than from the clue's own words is a hard Azed/Mephisto device; in the daily papers these are almost all a fodder leaf that swallowed the indicator or a link word ('[Cameron's first]CAMERONFIRST')
patterns.right: sel(V) over exactly the fodder words; the indicator belongs on the op

patterns.name: four or more mechanisms in one clue
patterns.why: four non-charade ops (nested containers with deletions and reversals, long acrostics) is more than a solver can unpick from a clue; real setters stop at two, occasionally three; the commonest are acrostics, double containers around acrostics, and one deletion written letter by letter, del(del(del(..))), that is really one op (an op nested four deep always lands here, so there is no separate depth rule)
patterns.right: fewer ops: merge repeated selections, flatten containers, or check the parse

patterns.name: unchecked node (parse not verified)
patterns.why: an op or leaf the validator could not rebuild step by step; its letters are taken as filed, so nothing says the shape is real (spoonerisms, cyclings, substitutions, reversals of part of a word and indirect anagrams are most of them)
patterns.right: re-annotate so every step is checked; none can be added now (the ratchet)

patterns.name: ordinary composition
patterns.why: checked ops composed to at most three mechanisms and three levels
